candidates.name: George Gipp
candidates.short_description: Notre Dame’s first Walter Camp All-American.
candidates.biography: George Gipp starred for Knute Rockne at Notre Dame as a versatile halfback, quarterback, and punter. His death at 25 and Rockne’s later ‘Win one for the Gipper’ speech turned an exceptional college career into an enduring piece of American sports culture.
candidates.why_interesting: The Upper Peninsula native became the athlete behind one of sports’ most famous rallying cries.

candidates.name: Frederic Baraga
candidates.short_description: Missionary and first bishop of Michigan’s Upper Peninsula.
candidates.biography: Frederic Baraga was a Slovenian Catholic missionary, grammarian, and author who worked in Native American languages. He became the first bishop of the church jurisdiction centered on Sault Ste. Marie and Marquette, and was declared venerable by Pope Benedict XVI in 2012.
candidates.why_interesting: His linguistic and missionary work connected the Upper Peninsula with immigrant communities and Native languages.

candidates.name: John D. Voelker
candidates.short_description: Michigan justice and author of Anatomy of a Murder.
candidates.biography: John D. Voelker was an Ishpeming lawyer, county prosecutor, Michigan Supreme Court justice, and writer under the name Robert Traver. His novel Anatomy of a Murder drew on a real Upper Peninsula case and became an acclaimed film starring James Stewart with music by Duke Ellington.
candidates.why_interesting: Few people have turned Upper Peninsula courtroom experience into a cultural landmark so successfully.

candidates.name: Dominic Jacobetti
candidates.short_description: Michigan’s longest-serving state representative.
candidates.biography: Dominic Jacobetti represented the western Upper Peninsula in the Michigan House from 1955 until his death in 1994. His nearly four decades in office remain the longest tenure in the chamber’s history.
candidates.why_interesting: His record-setting service made him one of the most durable political figures in Michigan history.

candidates.name: George Shiras III
candidates.short_description: Pioneer of nighttime wildlife photography.
candidates.biography: George Shiras III combined public service with groundbreaking nature photography. After serving in Congress, he became known for using trip wires and flash equipment to photograph wild animals at night, helping establish techniques later associated with camera traps.
candidates.why_interesting: He helped people see nocturnal wildlife decades before modern trail cameras.

candidates.name: Chase Osborn
candidates.short_description: Michigan governor, publisher, and explorer.
candidates.biography: Chase Osborn worked as a newspaper reporter and publisher, traveled as an explorer, and served as Michigan’s governor from 1911 to 1913. His unusually varied career connected public life in Michigan with writing and travel far beyond the state.
candidates.why_interesting: He brought the instincts of a newspaperman and explorer to Michigan’s governorship.

candidates.name: Bruce Catton
candidates.short_description: Pulitzer-winning historian of the Civil War.
candidates.biography: Bruce Catton was a journalist and narrative historian whose accessible books brought the American Civil War to a wide popular audience. A Stillness at Appomattox earned both the Pulitzer Prize for History and the National Book Award in 1954.
candidates.why_interesting: A writer from northern Michigan became one of America’s defining popular historians.

candidates.name: Bennie Oosterbaan
candidates.short_description: Three-sport Michigan star and national-title coach.
candidates.biography: Bennie Oosterbaan became an All-American in football and basketball at the University of Michigan while also excelling in baseball. He later coached the Wolverines to the 1948 national football championship and is remembered among the state’s greatest athletes.
candidates.why_interesting: His Michigan career spanned three varsity sports, multiple All-America honors, and a football national title as head coach.

candidates.name: Guy Vander Jagt
candidates.short_description: Congressman known as a commanding national speaker.
candidates.biography: Guy Vander Jagt was a lawyer, pastor, and Republican who represented western Michigan in Congress from 1966 to 1993. He also chaired the National Republican Congressional Committee and earned a national reputation for his public speaking.
candidates.why_interesting: His oratory made a long-serving Michigan congressman a sought-after voice on the national stage.

candidates.name: Ruth Thompson
candidates.short_description: Michigan lawyer and three-term U.S. representative.
candidates.biography: Ruth Thompson built a legal and political career before serving three terms in the U.S. House from 1951 to 1957. Her election placed a Michigan woman in Congress during an era when women remained rare in federal office.
candidates.why_interesting: Her congressional career marked an early breakthrough for Michigan women in national politics.

candidates.name: Whitcomb L. Judson
candidates.short_description: Inventor of an early zipper-style fastener.
candidates.biography: Whitcomb Judson was a mechanical engineer and prolific inventor who received thirty patents. His best-known clasp-locker, first intended for shoes and boots, became an important predecessor of the modern zipper.
candidates.why_interesting: A practical fastening idea helped lead to an object now used around the world every day.

candidates.name: Verna Aardema
candidates.short_description: Caldecott-winning children’s author.
candidates.biography: Verna Aardema adapted traditional stories and folklore, especially from Africa and Mexico, for young readers. Why Mosquitoes Buzz in People’s Ears won the 1976 Caldecott Medal, and several of her books received major children’s-literature honors.
candidates.why_interesting: Her storytelling introduced generations of children to folktales from cultures beyond their own.

candidates.name: Charles Hackley
candidates.short_description: Muskegon lumberman and civic philanthropist.
candidates.biography: Charles Hackley built his fortune in Michigan’s timber industry and became a major benefactor of Muskegon. His philanthropy helped support civic institutions that continued shaping the city long after the lumber era.
candidates.why_interesting: His name remains woven through Muskegon because he reinvested industrial wealth in the community.

candidates.name: Dirk J. Vlug
candidates.short_description: World War II Medal of Honor recipient.
candidates.biography: Dirk Vlug served in the United States Army during World War II. He received the Medal of Honor, the nation’s highest military decoration, for extraordinary actions in combat.
candidates.why_interesting: His wartime service earned the United States’ highest award for military valor.

candidates.name: Verne Troyer
candidates.short_description: Actor best known as Mini-Me in Austin Powers.
candidates.biography: Verne Troyer was an actor, comedian, stunt performer, and coordinator who became internationally recognizable as Mini-Me in the Austin Powers films. Standing 2 feet 8 inches because of cartilage–hair hypoplasia, he built a screen career that extended beyond the role that made him famous.
candidates.why_interesting: A performer from southwest Michigan became one of the most recognizable comedy-film figures of his era.

candidates.name: Charlie Maxwell
candidates.short_description: Two-time All-Star outfielder for the Detroit Tigers.
candidates.biography: Charlie Maxwell played fourteen Major League Baseball seasons, including eight with the Detroit Tigers. The left fielder made two American League All-Star teams and became known for his power hitting and unusually strong Sunday performances.
candidates.why_interesting: ‘Sunday Charlie’ became a memorable part of Tigers baseball in the 1950s and early 1960s.

candidates.name: Harry Blackstone, Jr.
candidates.short_description: Television-era stage magician and author.
candidates.biography: Harry Blackstone Jr. carried his family’s illusion tradition into television and modern stage performance. A prolific entertainer and author, he became famous for large-scale magic and for the countless rabbits produced during his career.
candidates.why_interesting: He brought classic American stage illusion to a new television generation.

candidates.name: Harry Blackstone, Sr.
candidates.short_description: Illusionist billed as The Great Blackstone.
candidates.biography: Harry Blackstone Sr., born Henry Boughton, became one of the twentieth century’s best-known stage magicians. He toured widely, entertained service members through the USO during World War II, and established a family legacy continued by his son.
candidates.why_interesting: His touring spectacles helped define the golden age of American stage magic.

candidates.name: Mary F. Thomas
candidates.short_description: Physician, abolitionist, and women’s-rights leader.
candidates.biography: Mary F. Thomas was a pioneering physician who worked for abolition, temperance, women’s property rights, and suffrage. She led state and national organizing, edited reform publications, and became the first woman to present a petition before the Indiana General Assembly.
candidates.why_interesting: She joined medicine, abolition, and suffrage into one unusually wide-ranging reform career.

candidates.name: Minnie Vautrin
candidates.short_description: Protected thousands during the Nanjing Massacre.
candidates.biography: Minnie Vautrin was an educator and missionary who spent twenty-eight years in China and led Ginling College. During the Nanjing Massacre she helped shelter and protect at least 10,000 refugees, documented events in a diary, and confronted occupying authorities on behalf of civilians.
candidates.why_interesting: Her college became a refuge because she repeatedly put herself between civilians and violence.

candidates.name: Herbert Henry Dow
candidates.short_description: Founder of Dow Chemical and chemical-process inventor.
candidates.biography: Herbert Henry Dow was a chemist, inventor, and industrialist who developed new ways to extract bromine from brine. He founded the company that became Dow Chemical, building a Michigan enterprise into a major force in the global chemical industry.
candidates.why_interesting: His experiments with Michigan brine helped create one of the state’s most influential companies.

candidates.name: Alden B. Dow
candidates.short_description: Architect who shaped Michigan modernism.
candidates.biography: Alden B. Dow built a prolific architectural practice in Midland and became a leading voice in Michigan Modern design. His homes, schools, churches, civic buildings, and cultural projects reshaped his hometown and extended his influence across the state.
candidates.why_interesting: His inventive buildings gave Midland one of America’s most distinctive modern architectural landscapes.

candidates.name: Jim Northrup
candidates.short_description: Outfielder on the 1968 world-champion Detroit Tigers.
candidates.biography: Jim Northrup spent most of his Major League Baseball career with the Detroit Tigers. The left-handed outfielder became a key member of the 1968 championship club and remained closely identified with that celebrated team.
candidates.why_interesting: He helped deliver one of the most beloved championships in Detroit sports history.

candidates.name: Merze Tate
candidates.short_description: Barrier-breaking scholar of American diplomacy.
candidates.biography: Merze Tate became the first Black graduate of Western Michigan Teachers College and the first Black woman to attend Oxford. She later became the first Black woman to earn a doctorate in government and international relations from Harvard and built a distinguished career at Howard University.
candidates.why_interesting: Her academic firsts opened doors across Michigan, Oxford, Harvard, and the study of international relations.

candidates.name: Theodore Roethke
candidates.short_description: Pulitzer- and National Book Award-winning poet.
candidates.biography: Theodore Roethke became one of the most influential American poets of his generation, known for rhythmic work rich in natural imagery and introspection. He won the Pulitzer Prize for The Waking and received two National Book Awards for poetry.
candidates.why_interesting: A poet raised among Saginaw greenhouses transformed the natural world into nationally honored verse.

candidates.name: Kid Lavigne
candidates.short_description: First widely recognized world lightweight boxing champion.
candidates.biography: George ‘Kid’ Lavigne rose from Bay City to become boxing’s first widely recognized world lightweight champion. He claimed the vacant title in 1896 during the sport’s rough early professional era.
candidates.why_interesting: A Bay City fighter helped establish the lineage of a major world boxing championship.

candidates.name: Deacon McGuire
candidates.short_description: Record-setting catcher with a 26-season career.
candidates.biography: Deacon McGuire played twenty-six Major League Baseball seasons between 1883 and 1912 and later managed and coached. The durable catcher set numerous career records at his position, with several defensive totals still standing.
candidates.why_interesting: His longevity behind the plate produced records that survived more than a century of baseball.

candidates.name: Otto Frederick Rohwedder
candidates.short_description: Inventor of the commercial bread-slicing machine.
candidates.biography: Otto Rohwedder was an engineer and inventor who created the first automatic machine to slice bread for commercial sale. Its successful use by a Missouri bakery helped turn pre-sliced loaves into an everyday consumer standard.
candidates.why_interesting: His machine made ‘the greatest thing since sliced bread’ possible in the first place.

candidates.name: John Jay Shipherd
candidates.short_description: Co-founder of Oberlin and founder of Olivet College.
candidates.biography: John Jay Shipherd was a clergyman who co-founded Oberlin College and later founded Olivet College in Michigan. He envisioned schools built around community service and manual labor; Oberlin went on to set early precedents for interracial and coeducational admission.
candidates.why_interesting: Two colleges grew from his unusually inclusive vision of education and community.

candidates.name: Bob Burman
candidates.short_description: Early racing speed-record holder and Indianapolis 500 driver.
candidates.biography: Bob Burman was a pioneering American racing driver who set multiple speed records in the early twentieth century. He competed in many formative events in auto racing, including the first Indianapolis 500 in 1911.
candidates.why_interesting: He pushed automotive speed limits when organized racing was still being invented.
